payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the background into a basketball court
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image show the background changed into a basketball court?
node.criteria: Pass if the background itself is recognizably a basketball court, supported by visible court context such as a playing surface and court markings; basketball equipment may support this judgment but equipment alone is insufficient. Fail if the background is clearly not a basketball court. Unknown if the background cannot be assessed reliably.
node.binding: Judge whether the requested background replacement is complete: the background must read as a basketball court, not merely contain basketball-related objects.

node_traces.evidence: The background has been changed from a kitchen and includes basketball hoops and balls, but it does not read as a basketball court: there is no recognizable court surface or visible court markings beyond a single line.

The kitchen background has been replaced with a dark basketball-themed scene, but it does not read as a basketball court: there is no recognizable playing surface with court markings. The hoops and basketballs alone are insufficient.

The kitchen background has been replaced with basketball-related objects, including a hoop and basketballs, but the background does not read as a basketball court: there is no recognizable court playing surface or clear court markings.
The background shows a basketball hoop and a playing surface with visible court markings, so it reads as a basketball court.

The edited background shows a basketball hoop and balls, but the surrounding area is a plain dark backdrop with no recognizable basketball-court playing surface or markings. Basketball equipment alone does not establish a court.

fulfillment: The binding is truncated and underspecified (“The background (...) a basketball court”), leaving the completion criterion to drift across checks. Clarify that completion means the edited background reads as a basketball court, using the visible playing surface and court markings as evidence; basketball equipment alone is not sufficient. Keep progress separate from completion: s2 may establish requested progress, but cannot override s1’s completion judgment. The traces repeatedly call the same kind of scene partial when s1 fails and s2 passes, while the edited image visibly has a court surface and line markings as well as a hoop and balls; this suggests the completion check may be applying an unstated or inconsistent threshold. Align s1 and s2 on what visible evidence establishes a court, and have the aggregate resolve their evidence consistently rather than treating contradictory judgments as uncertainty. Preserve unknown for genuinely insufficient or conflicting visual evidence. All traces are valid and queried, so this is a semantic criterion/binding issue, not a transport or dependency failure.
s2: The node’s “incomplete change” condition is ambiguous and conflates progress with completion. In the edited image, the kitchen is replaced by a clearly recognizable basketball-court setting: hoop and net, playing surface, and court lines are visible. That is strong evidence of completed fulfillment, not merely partial progress. Keep this support node narrowly about whether any requested progress occurred; do not make it fail just because the change is complete. Align its criterion and binding with the parent completion check so a complete court still passes this progress check, while completion is decided separately. Treat equipment alone without a changed court background as insufficient evidence of background progress. The repeated high-confidence pass/fail split is semantic criterion drift, not transport or dependency failure; preserve unknown only for genuinely unassessable evidence.
